findings.issue: The root-level `sudo -n kill -- -<pgid>` can fire without a fresh groupExists check. In the killAfterSeconds timer (lines 138-140), stopGroup(pid, 'SIGTERM'/'SIGKILL') runs without first checking that the group still exists. Inside reap() the check comes before stopGroup, but a small window remains before the sudo call. If every member of the group has exited and the kernel has reused the pgid for a new group leader, a root kill would hit an unrelated process group.
findings.evidence: pgid comes from child.pid (trusted, not attacker-controlled) -> killGroup gets EPERM -> sudoKillGroup -> `sudo kill -s KILL -- -pgid` as root. There is no attacker-controlled input. Reuse needs the group to empty and the pid to be recycled within milliseconds to about 2 s on an ephemeral CI runner. The risk is theoretical, so there is no reachable exploit.
findings.fix: Optional: in stopGroup, call groupExists(pid) right before sudoKill. Skip the sudo call when it returns false (ESRCH). That way the sudo kill only follows an EPERM on a group that is confirmed live.

findings.issue: The test cleanup runs `sudo -n pkill -KILL -f` with an unanchored regex. It matches any root-visible command line that contains the marker substring. The marker is a random 9-digit value, so a collision is practically impossible. It runs only on Linux CI.
findings.evidence: The marker comes from crypto.randomInt and is not untrusted input. The pattern is passed as an argv element with no shell. The worst case is SIGKILL of an unrelated CI process whose command line happens to contain the marker.
findings.fix: Optional: anchor the pattern to the expected argv tail, e.g. `sleep [1]000[.]NNN$`, so that only the test's own sleep and sh processes can match.

summary: The change adds a privileged `sudo -n kill` fallback in tools/ci/retry.js and `sudo -n pkill` cleanup in a test that runs only on Linux CI. Both are invoked through spawnSync with an argv array and no shell. The pgid is a number taken from child.pid and the signal names are internal constants, so there is no injection. `-n` fails closed and never prompts. The log lines contain only pids and signal names, so no secrets are exposed, and there are no new dependencies. The sudo spawnSync call is bounded by a 10 s timeout and the reap loop by 2 s. No untrusted input reaches the new code, so there are no BLOCKER or MAJOR findings. One MINOR finding: a pgid-reuse window before the root kill. One NIT: the test's pkill regex is unanchored.
